newsitem.title: USA: Weak yen to fuel Japan trade surplus surge - study.
newsitem.headline: Weak yen to fuel Japan trade surplus surge - study.

text.p: A recently released econometric study by consulting firm I.D.E.A. Inc forecasts a significant climb in Japan's trade surplus based on persistent weakness in the yen.

Under the current exchange rate environment, Japan's trade surplus is expected to push up to 11.8 trillion yen in 1997 and 14.1 trillion yen in 1998, according to the study. Japan's trade surplus totalled 9.1 trillion yen in 1996.

The report found Japan's goods trade balance to be "extremely sensitive" to changes in the real effective yen exchange rate. The U.S.-Japan bilateral balance was similarly sensitive to shifts in dollar/yen.

"A 10 percent change in the real yen effective exchange rate is estimated to increase the annualized Japanese trade surplus by some $28 billion, with the full impact felt over three years," the study said.

The dollar is currently trading at roughly 126 yen, close to a four-and-a-half year high of 127.19 reached earlier this month. It has appreciated by over 50 percent against the yen over the past two years and by roughly 10 percent since the beginning of this year.

The study said the peak influence from exchange rate moves came after 22 months and that the J-curve effect -- whereby an exchange rate depreciation initially results in a modest decrease in the trade surplus -- lasted for eight months.

The cumulative impact of exchange rate depreciation was found to help the trade balance on a year-on-year comparison only after 15 months -- the reason why it was only in the fourth quarter of last year that signs of a rise in the Japanese trade surplus were apparent.

Assuming unchanged exchange rates, conservative projections of the U.S.-Japan bilateral balance suggest that Japan's surplus will increase from an underlying annualized rate of close to four trillion yen to six trillion yen by the end of the year, and to seven trillion yen by the end of 1998, the report said.

Trade equations in the study suggested that Japanese domestic demand would have to be expanded by at least one percent for every four percent dollar devaluation against the yen to have the equivalent influence on the trade balance
I.D.E.A. predicted that the implications for G2 foreign exchange politics would be great in the year ahead.

"While we regard the Rubin policy of not using the dollar as a trade-tool as heart-felt, it will also become impossible for the U.S. Treasury to ignore the ramifications of price competitiveness of a yen that has in real effective terms devalued nearly 20 percent from its five-year average," the study, authored by chief economist Alan Ruskin, said.

"Clearly there are severe limits to how much Japan can be expected to expand domestic demand to correct the trade balance, and the exchange rate is likely to become the central plank in any policy attempts to reduce Japan's trade surplus."
At a meeting between President Clinton and Japanese Prime Minister Ryutaro Hashimoto on Friday, Japan tried to quell U.S. concerns about recent gains in Japan's trade surplus.

In recent weeks, U.S. administration officials, including Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin, have repeatedly called on Japan to stimulate domestic demand and avoid over-reliance on exports as a source of growth.
